definition: Feeling or showing strong, eager enthusiasm or devotion.
example: Her grandfather was an ardent collector of old maps and spent his weekends searching estate sales.
nuance: Ardent suggests warm, glowing devotion, while zealous can hint at excessive or single-minded intensity; don't confuse it with arduous, "difficult."
prompt: A student joins the school's astronomy club.
options: As an ardent stargazer, Maya stayed up past midnight to log every meteor.
The ardent climb to the observatory roof left the club members gasping for air.
Leo was an ardent club member who skipped meetings and never glanced at the sky.
The club's ardent telescope sat unused in a closet all winter.
reasons: Staying up late to track meteors shows eager, heartfelt commitment to the hobby.
This confuses the word with arduous; a steep climb is hard, not passionate.
Skipping meetings and ignoring the sky shows indifference, the reverse of strong enthusiasm.
An unused instrument has no feelings, so it cannot be eager or devoted.

practice.prompt: A town is restoring its old public library.
options: The ardent residents shrugged and said they didn't care if the library ever reopened.
The librarian gave an ardent nod, barely looking up from her lukewarm coffee.
Ardent volunteers spent every Saturday repainting shelves and sorting donated books.
Restoring the library was an ardent task that took three exhausting years.
reasons: Not caring about the outcome is apathy, the opposite of eager devotion.
A distracted, half-hearted nod lacks the intense feeling the word requires.
Giving up every weekend for unpaid work shows wholehearted dedication to the cause.
Here the word is mistaken for arduous; a task can be tiring but cannot feel passion.
